title: Erik Erikson: Identity Theory
overview: Erik Erikson, trained by Anna Freud and never holding a university degree, extended psychoanalysis in three ways: personality develops over the whole life span, the ego is independent of the id, and culture and history shape personality. Drawing on his own identity crises, he described eight psychosocial stages governed by the epigenetic principle, each built around a crisis (trust vs. mistrust through ego integrity vs. despair) whose balanced, mainly adaptive resolution yields a basic strength (hope, will, purpose, competence, fidelity, love, care, wisdom), while one-sided resolution produces maladaptive or malignant maldevelopment. His image of human nature is optimistic and only partly deterministic. He assessed personality through play therapy, anthropological studies and psychohistorical analysis, and later researchers built tests such as the Loyola Generativity Scale. Research supports early trust, the stage sequence, Marcia's identity statuses, and the benefits of generativity and ego integrity, and extends the theory to virtual, gender, ethnic (Cross model) and gender preference identity. Critics cite vague concepts, a thin account of old age, biased views on sex differences and limited fit to women and poorer people.
objectives: Explain the three ways in which Erikson extended Freud's theory.
Relate Erikson's personal identity crises to the concepts of his theory, including identity confusion.
Explain the epigenetic principle of maturation, the nature of crises, adaptive coping and basic strengths.
Describe each of the eight psychosocial stages with its ages, crisis, basic strength and parallel Freudian stage (Table 6.1).
Distinguish maladaptive from malignant maldevelopment and name the tendencies for each stage (Table 6.2).
Describe Erikson's image of human nature and contrast it with Freud's.
Describe Erikson's assessment methods: play therapy, psychohistorical analysis, anthropological studies, and tests based on his theory.
Summarise research on trust, the stages, Marcia's identity statuses, sex differences, virtual identity, gender, generativity and maturity.
Explain research on racial and ethnic identity, including Cross's model, and on gender preference identity.
Evaluate Erikson's contributions, criticisms and influence.

sections.heading: Introduction: How Erikson Extended Freud
sections.detailed:
Erik Erikson is one of the rare personality theorists who became a public celebrity. His books sold widely and he featured on the covers of Newsweek and the New York Times Magazine, yet he never earned a university degree in any subject. He was trained in the Freudian tradition by Anna Freud, and he always treated psychoanalysis as his starting point. Anderson and Friedman describe him as someone who presented himself as a loyal Freudian while moving a long way from orthodox theory.

The chapter identifies three ways in which Erikson extended Freud's work. This list is a standard exam question (it also answers Review Question 2 on how the two theories differ).

First, he elaborated Freud's developmental stages and argued that personality keeps developing across the entire life span, not just in the first five or six years. Freud's stages end with the genital stage; Erikson's eight stages run from birth to old age.

Second, he gave greater weight to the ego than to the id. For Erikson the ego is an independent part of personality; it is not a servant of the id as Freud had claimed. This is why his approach is often described as an ego psychology and why the key concept of his theory is ego identity.

Third, he recognised the influence of cultural and historical forces on personality. Innate biological factors operating in childhood matter, but they do not fully explain personality; we are not governed entirely by them.

So Erikson kept the core of Freud (stages, unconscious conflict, the Oedipal situation, the superego) while broadening its scope in time (whole life span), in structure (independent ego) and in context (culture and history). The book places him under the life-span approach for this reason.
sections.simple: Erikson was trained by Anna Freud and saw himself as a Freudian, but he changed Freud's theory in three big ways. He said personality develops across the whole life span, he made the ego independent of the id, and he showed that culture and history shape personality, not just biology.
keyPoints: Erikson became famous without any university degree; trained by Anna Freud.
Extension 1: development continues over the entire life span (eight stages).
Extension 2: the ego is independent, not subservient to the id.
Extension 3: cultural and historical forces affect personality; biology alone does not explain it.
He kept psychoanalysis as his starting point while departing substantially from orthodoxy.

sections.heading: The Life of Erikson (1902–1994)
sections.detailed:
Erikson's life is a textbook case of a theory growing out of the theorist's own experience. Wallerstein notes that he went through several identity crises that he never fully resolved.

Personal identity crises. He was born in Frankfurt, Germany. His Danish mother came from a wealthy Jewish family; her husband vanished within hours of their wedding, and she later became pregnant by another man and was sent to Germany to avoid the disgrace of an illegitimate birth. She never told Erik who his father was, despite his pleading. She then married Dr. Theodore Homburger, the baby's pediatrician. Erik learned only later that Homburger was not his biological father and said he grew up unsure of his name and psychological identity. He kept the name Homburger until 37, when he became a U.S. citizen and renamed himself Erik Homburger Erikson. At school he faced a second identity crisis: German classmates rejected him because his family was Jewish, while Jewish classmates rejected him because he was tall and blond with Aryan features. His grades were mediocre but he had artistic talent.

Dropping out of society. After high school he dropped out of conventional life and wandered through Europe, reading, keeping a notebook and observing people. He saw himself as morbidly sensitive and neurotic, even close to psychotic. His daughter Bloland later wrote that he suffered deeply from feeling abandoned by his real father, struggled with depression all his life, and craved reassurance. He attended two art schools and exhibited in Munich but kept leaving to continue his search for identity. He himself joked that he needed to name the identity crisis and see it in everyone else in order to deal with it in himself. Friedman observed that what Erikson experienced personally became the "research" behind his ideas.

Becoming a Freudian. At 25 he was invited to teach at a small Vienna school for the children of Freud's patients and friends. He admitted he was partly drawn to Freud in search of a father, and here he felt he had finally found an identity. He was analysed by Anna Freud almost daily for three years (for $7 a month). Her interest in child analysis, plus his teaching, focused him on child development and social influences. He became a member of the Vienna Psychoanalytic Institute.

Three marriages and a stable foundation. In 1929 he met Joan Serson, a Canadian-born artist and dancer. When she became pregnant he at first refused to marry her, fearing commitment and parental disapproval; friends convinced him he would be repeating his own father's behaviour. He then married her three times, in Jewish, Protestant and civil ceremonies. Joan gave up her career to become his lifelong intellectual partner and editor and gave him a stable foundation; his half-sister said he would have been nothing without her, and he agreed.

Coming to America. In 1933, with the Nazi threat growing, the Eriksons moved to Denmark and then Boston, where he practised child psychoanalysis, worked with delinquents and at Massachusetts General Hospital. He failed his first course in Harvard's Ph.D. programme and dropped out, yet in 1936 Yale's Institute of Human Relations invited him, degree-less, to teach in its medical school. With a Yale anthropologist he studied child-rearing among South Dakota's Sioux, which strengthened his belief in culture's influence. He continued at Berkeley's Institute of Human Development and deliberately sought patients from diverse cultures and normal as well as disturbed people.

Honors and accolades, but no identity. Among American Indians in South Dakota and California he saw symptoms that orthodox Freudian theory could not explain: alienation from cultural traditions producing an unclear self-image. He first called this identity confusion and saw the same pattern in disturbed World War II veterans, whom he judged to be suffering not from repressed conflicts but from confusion caused by trauma and being uprooted from their culture. In 1950 he joined the Austen Riggs Center (for disturbed adolescents); ten years later he returned to Harvard to teach on the human life cycle, retiring in 1970. At 84 he published a book on old age. Despite his fame, his daughter reported he remained ashamed of having been an illegitimate child.
sections.simple: Erikson never knew his real father, was raised by a stepfather, and was rejected by both German and Jewish classmates, so he grew up unsure who he was. He wandered Europe as an artist before Anna Freud trained him in Vienna. In America, studying Sioux children and war veterans, he spotted "identity confusion", which became central to his theory.
keyPoints: Illegitimate birth, unknown father and stepfather Homburger: lifelong uncertainty about name and identity.
Rejected at school by German peers (Jewish family) and Jewish peers (Aryan looks).
Wandered Europe as an artist; analysed by Anna Freud in Vienna, where he found an identity.
Wife Joan Serson was his intellectual partner and stable foundation.
No degree, yet taught at Yale and Harvard; studied the Sioux with an anthropologist.
Observed identity confusion in American Indians and WWII veterans: cultural uprooting, not repressed conflict.

sections.heading: Psychosocial Stages of Personality Development: Genetics, Crises, Coping and Strengths
sections.detailed:
Erikson divided personality growth into eight psychosocial stages that cover the whole life span. The first four parallel Freud's oral, anal, phallic and latency stages, but the key difference is emphasis: Erikson stressed psychosocial correlates of each stage, while Freud stressed biological ones. At every stage we must cope with a crisis in either an adaptive or a maladaptive way.

The role of genetics and the environment. Development follows what Erikson called the epigenetic principle of maturation. Inherited forces determine the stages themselves and their sequence; the prefix epi means "upon", signalling that development rests upon genetic factors. But social and environmental forces control how these genetically predetermined stages are actually realised. Personality is therefore shaped jointly by biological and social factors (this answers Review Question 4).

Conflicts and crises. Development is a series of personal conflicts. The potential for each conflict is present at birth as an innate predisposition, and each becomes prominent at a particular stage when the environment demands a certain adaptation. Each such confrontation with the environment is a crisis: a turning point that requires a shift in perspective and a refocusing of instinctual energy to suit that stage. We can respond in a maladaptive (negative) or adaptive (positive) way. Only when a conflict is resolved can personality move on normally and gain strength for the next crisis. An unresolved conflict makes later adaptation harder, though a successful outcome remains possible.

Adaptive coping. Erikson held that the ego must incorporate both the adaptive and the maladaptive ways of coping. In infancy, for example, the crisis of helplessness and dependency can produce trust or mistrust. Trust is clearly healthier, but some mistrust is protective: a totally trusting, gullible person is easily deceived and manipulated. Ideally the ego consists mainly of the positive attitude balanced by some of the negative one; only then is the crisis satisfactorily resolved.

Basic strengths. Each stage also offers the chance to develop a basic strength or virtue, which emerges once the crisis is satisfactorily resolved. The strengths are interdependent: a strength cannot develop until the strength of the previous stage has been confirmed. Table 6.1 summarises the scheme:

Oral-sensory (birth–1): trust vs. mistrust, hope. Muscular-anal (1–3): autonomy vs. doubt and shame, will. Locomotor-genital (3–5): initiative vs. guilt, purpose. Latency (6–11): industriousness vs. inferiority, competence. Adolescence (12–18): identity cohesion vs. role confusion, fidelity. Young adulthood (18–35): intimacy vs. isolation, love. Adulthood (35–55): generativity vs. stagnation, care. Maturity and old age (55+): ego integrity vs. despair, wisdom.
sections.simple: Erikson's eight stages run from birth to old age. Genes fix the order of the stages, but the social environment decides how each turns out. Every stage has a crisis that can be handled well or badly; handling it well (with a little of the negative side kept for balance) produces a basic strength such as hope or love.
keyPoints: Eight psychosocial stages; first four parallel Freud's but stress social, not biological, factors.
Epigenetic principle: genes set the stages; environment determines how they are realised.
Crisis = turning point at each stage; resolved adaptively or maladaptively.
Healthy ego = mostly adaptive attitude plus some of the maladaptive one (e.g., a little mistrust).
Basic strengths (hope, will, purpose, competence, fidelity, love, care, wisdom) are interdependent.

sections.heading: Trust versus Mistrust
sections.detailed:
The oral-sensory stage covers the first year of life and parallels Freud's oral stage. It is the period of greatest helplessness: the infant depends totally on the mother or primary caregiver for survival, security and affection. The mouth is central; Erikson said the infant lives and loves through the mouth. But the infant–world relationship is social as well as biological, and the baby's interaction with the mother decides whether trust or mistrust is built into personality.

It's up to the mother. If the mother meets the baby's physical needs appropriately and gives plenty of affection, love and security, the infant develops trust, an attitude that colours how the growing child sees self and others. We learn to expect consistency, continuity and sameness from people and situations, and Erikson saw this expectation as the beginning of ego identity. If the mother is rejecting, inattentive or inconsistent, the infant may develop mistrust and become suspicious, fearful and anxious. Erikson also argued that mistrust can arise when the mother lacks an exclusive focus on the child; he claimed that a new mother who returns to an outside job and leaves the baby with relatives or in day care risks promoting mistrust.

Trust can be lost later in life. Although the trust–mistrust pattern is set in infancy, the issue can resurface later. A high level of trust from an ideal mother–infant relationship can be destroyed if the mother dies or leaves, and mistrust may take over. Equally, childhood mistrust can be reversed later through a loving, patient teacher or friend.

Hope. Successful resolution yields the basic strength of hope: the belief that our desires will be satisfied, a persistent feeling of confidence maintained despite temporary setbacks.

In Table 6.2, too much trust (with no mistrust) produces the maladaptive tendency sensory maladjustment; too much mistrust produces the malignant tendency withdrawal.
sections.simple: In the first year the baby depends completely on the mother. Consistent, loving care builds trust; rejecting or inconsistent care builds mistrust. Trust can still be lost or regained later, and resolving this stage gives the strength of hope.
keyPoints: Oral-sensory stage, birth to 1 year; parallels Freud's oral stage.
Mother's consistent, affectionate care produces trust and the start of ego identity.
Rejecting, inattentive or inconsistent mothering (or lack of exclusive focus) produces mistrust.
The pattern can change later: loss of a mother can destroy trust; a patient friend can repair mistrust.
Basic strength: hope, a persistent confidence that desires will be satisfied.

sections.heading: Autonomy versus Doubt and Shame
sections.detailed:
The muscular-anal stage covers the second and third years of life and corresponds to Freud's anal stage. Children rapidly develop physical and mental abilities: they communicate better, walk, climb, push, pull, and hold on to or let go of objects. They are proud of these skills and want to do as much as possible for themselves.

Erikson considered holding on and letting go the most important of these abilities, because they are prototypes for how we respond to later conflicts. Holding on can be loving or hostile; letting go can be a release of destructive rage or a relaxed passivity.

Choice. The key feature of this stage is that, for the first time, children can exercise some choice and feel the power of their autonomous will. Still dependent, they begin to see themselves as persons in their own right. The crucial question is how far society, in the form of the parents, will let them express themselves and do what they are capable of.

The toilet-training crisis. The main parent–child clash typically concerns toilet training, the first time society tries to regulate an instinctual need: the child must hold on and let go only at the right times and places. Parents may let the child progress at his or her own pace, or they may become annoyed, force the training and react with impatience and anger. When parents frustrate the child's attempts at independence in this way, the child develops self-doubt and a sense of shame in dealing with others. Although the anal region is the focus, the conflict is expressed more psychosocially than biologically.

Will. The basic strength arising from autonomy is will: a determination to exercise freedom of choice and self-restraint in the face of society's demands.

Maldevelopment (Table 6.2): excessive autonomy leads to shameless willfulness; excessive doubt and shame leads to compulsion.
sections.simple: Between ages 1 and 3 toddlers can walk, talk and choose for themselves for the first time. Toilet training is the big test: patient parents foster autonomy, while forcing and angry parents produce doubt and shame. Success gives the strength of will.
keyPoints: Muscular-anal stage, ages 1–3; parallels Freud's anal stage.
Holding on and letting go are prototypes for later reactions to conflict.
First chance to exercise choice and autonomous will.
Toilet training is the key crisis; forcing it breeds self-doubt and shame.
Basic strength: will, the determination to exercise free choice and self-restraint.

sections.heading: Initiative versus Guilt
sections.detailed:
The locomotor-genital stage, from about 3 to 5 years, resembles Freud's phallic stage. Motor and mental abilities keep growing, children can do more on their own, and they show a strong desire to take the initiative in many activities.

The Oedipal relationship. One form of initiative appears in fantasies: the wish to possess the opposite-sex parent and to rival the same-sex parent. The decisive factor is the parents' reaction to these self-initiated activities and fantasies. If parents punish the child and otherwise inhibit initiative, the child develops persistent guilt that will affect self-directed activity throughout life. The child inevitably fails in the Oedipal relationship, but if parents handle the situation with love and understanding, the child learns what is and is not permissible. Initiative can then be channelled into realistic, socially approved goals, preparing for adult responsibility and morality; in Freudian terms this is the superego.

Purpose. The basic strength arising from initiative is purpose, the courage to envision and pursue goals.

Maldevelopment (Table 6.2): excessive initiative leads to ruthlessness; excessive guilt leads to inhibition.
sections.simple: From 3 to 5, children want to start things on their own, including Oedipal fantasies. If parents punish this initiative the child carries lasting guilt; if they guide it lovingly, the child learns limits and develops purpose, the courage to chase goals.
keyPoints: Locomotor-genital stage, ages 3–5; parallels Freud's phallic stage.
Strong desire to take initiative; includes Oedipal fantasies.
Punishing parents create persistent guilt; loving guidance channels initiative toward approved goals.
This channelling corresponds to Freud's superego (responsibility and morality).
Basic strength: purpose, the courage to envision and pursue goals.

sections.heading: Industriousness versus Inferiority
sections.detailed:
Erikson's latency stage runs from 6 to 11 and corresponds to Freud's latency period. The child starts school and meets new social influences. Ideally the child learns good work and study habits at home and school, which Erikson called industriousness, mainly as a way to win praise and the satisfaction of completing a task.

Developing new skills. Growing deductive reasoning and the ability to play by rules lead children to deliberately refine skills shown in building things. Here Erikson's views reflected the sex stereotypes of his era: boys build tree houses and model airplanes, girls cook and sew. Whatever the activity, children now make serious attempts to complete tasks with concentrated attention, diligence and persistence; in Erikson's words they begin learning the basic skills of technology, the tools of the "big people".

Parents' and teachers' attitudes largely determine how children judge their own developing skills. Scolding, ridicule or rejection create feelings of inferiority and inadequacy; praise and reinforcement foster competence and continued effort.

Competence. The basic strength emerging from industriousness is competence: applying skill and intelligence to pursue and complete tasks.

The final four developmental stages (major contrast, Review Question 9). The outcome of each of the first four childhood stages depends on other people; it is more a matter of what is done to children than of what they can do for themselves. Even though independence grows from birth to 11, development stays mostly under the influence of parents and teachers. In the last four stages we gain increasing control over our environment, consciously choosing friends, colleges, careers, spouses and leisure activities. Yet these choices are shaped by the characteristics formed in the earlier stages: whether the ego shows mainly trust, autonomy, initiative and industriousness, or mistrust, doubt, guilt and inferiority, will determine the course of the rest of life.

Maldevelopment (Table 6.2): excessive industriousness leads to narrow virtuosity; excessive inferiority leads to inertia.
sections.simple: From 6 to 11, school-age children learn to work hard and finish tasks. Praise from parents and teachers builds competence; scolding and ridicule build inferiority. In the first four stages others shape the outcome, whereas in the last four we increasingly choose for ourselves, though early outcomes still steer those choices.
keyPoints: Latency stage, ages 6–11; school brings new social influences.
Industriousness = good work and study habits, pursued for praise and task satisfaction.
Erikson's examples reflected the sex stereotypes of his period.
Praise fosters competence; scolding and ridicule foster inferiority.
Basic strength: competence. First four stages depend on others; last four allow more conscious choice.

sections.heading: Identity Cohesion versus Role Confusion
sections.detailed:
Adolescence, from 12 to 18, is the stage at which the crisis of basic ego identity must be met and resolved. This is when we form our self-image, integrating our ideas about ourselves with what others think of us. Satisfactory resolution produces a consistent, congruent picture of the self.

Shaping and accepting an identity is difficult and often anxious work. Adolescents experiment with different roles and ideologies to find the best fit. Erikson saw adolescence as a hiatus between childhood and adulthood: a necessary psychological moratorium that gives the person time and energy to play different roles and live with different self-images.

The identity crisis. Those who leave this stage with a strong sense of identity can face adulthood with certainty and confidence. Those who fail to achieve a cohesive identity, experiencing what Erikson called an identity crisis, show role confusion: they do not know who or what they are, where they belong or where they want to go. They may withdraw from the normal life sequence of education, job and marriage, as Erikson himself did for a time, or seek a negative identity in crime or drugs. A negative identity, as society defines it, is still preferable to no identity at all, though less satisfying than a positive one.

Erikson stressed the strong impact of peer groups on ego identity. Excessive association with fanatical groups and cults, or obsessive identification with popular-culture icons, can restrict the developing ego.

Fidelity. The basic strength of adolescence is fidelity, emerging from a cohesive ego identity. It includes sincerity, genuineness and a sense of duty in relationships with others.

Maldevelopment (Table 6.2): excessive identity cohesion leads to fanaticism; excessive role confusion leads to repudiation.

Factors affecting identity (Review Question 10): the outcomes of the four earlier stages, peer groups, the opportunity for a moratorium, and the social and historical context all matter; people fail when earlier crises were badly resolved or when they cannot experiment and integrate a self-image.
sections.simple: From 12 to 18, teens must work out who they are by trying on different roles during a "moratorium". Success gives a stable identity and the strength of fidelity; failure, the identity crisis, leaves role confusion, dropping out or a negative identity such as crime or drugs. Peer groups strongly shape the result.
keyPoints: Adolescence, ages 12–18; the crisis of ego identity.
Ego identity integrates our ideas of ourselves with what others think of us.
Psychological moratorium: time to experiment with roles and ideologies.
Identity crisis leads to role confusion, withdrawal, or a negative identity (better than none).
Peers matter; cults or obsessive celebrity identification can restrict the ego.
Basic strength: fidelity (sincerity, genuineness, sense of duty).

sections.heading: Intimacy versus Isolation
sections.detailed:
Erikson considered young adulthood a longer stage than the earlier ones, stretching from the end of adolescence to about 35. In it we establish independence from parents and quasi-parental institutions such as college, and start to function autonomously as mature, responsible adults. We take up productive work and form intimate relationships, typically close friendships and sexual unions.

Caring and commitment. Intimacy for Erikson was not limited to sex; it includes caring and commitment. These feelings can be shown openly, without self-protective defences and without fear of losing one's identity. In true intimacy we can merge our identity with another person's without submerging or losing it. (This depends on having first achieved a secure identity in adolescence.)

People who cannot form such intimacies develop feelings of isolation. They avoid social contact, reject others and may even become aggressive toward them. They prefer to be alone because they fear intimacy as a threat to their ego identity.

Love. The basic strength of young adulthood is love, which Erikson regarded as the greatest of all human virtues. He described it as mutual devotion in a shared identity, the fusing of oneself with another person.

Maldevelopment (Table 6.2): excessive intimacy leads to promiscuity; excessive isolation leads to exclusivity.
sections.simple: From about 18 to 35, young adults become independent, start working and form close friendships and partnerships. Real intimacy means sharing your identity with someone without losing it. People who fear intimacy become isolated; success brings love, which Erikson called the greatest virtue.
keyPoints: Young adulthood, roughly 18–35; a longer stage than earlier ones.
Independence from parents and institutions; productive work and intimate relationships.
Intimacy includes caring and commitment, not just sex; merging identity without losing it.
Isolation: avoiding or rejecting others, even aggression, from fear that intimacy threatens identity.
Basic strength: love, the greatest human virtue, a mutual devotion in shared identity.

sections.heading: Generativity versus Stagnation
sections.detailed:
Adulthood, roughly ages 35 to 55, is a stage of maturity in which we need to be actively involved in teaching and guiding the next generation. This need goes beyond one's own family: concern becomes broader and longer-range, extending to future generations and the kind of society they will live in. One does not have to be a parent to show generativity, and having children does not automatically satisfy the urge.

Erikson believed that all institutions, whether business, government, social service or academic, offer outlets for generativity. In almost any organisation or activity we can find ways to act as a mentor, teacher or guide to younger people for the good of society.

When middle-aged people cannot or will not find an outlet for generativity, they may be overwhelmed by stagnation, boredom and interpersonal impoverishment. This picture resembles Jung's description of the midlife crisis. Such people may regress to pseudo-intimacy, indulging themselves in childlike ways, and may become physical or psychological invalids through absorption in their own needs and comforts.

Care. The basic strength of adulthood is care, defined as a broad concern for others. Erikson saw it expressed in the need to teach, not only to help others but also to fulfil one's own identity.

Example of achieving generativity (Review Question 12): mentoring junior colleagues at work, teaching, guiding young people through a social-service organisation, or raising and guiding children.

Maldevelopment (Table 6.2): excessive generativity leads to overextension; excessive stagnation leads to rejectivity.
sections.simple: From 35 to 55, adults need to guide and teach the next generation, through parenting, work, mentoring or community roles. Those who do not become stagnant, bored and self-absorbed, similar to Jung's midlife crisis. Success brings the strength of care.
keyPoints: Adulthood, about 35–55; need to teach and guide the next generation.
Generativity extends beyond one's family; parenthood is neither necessary nor sufficient.
All institutions offer outlets (mentor, teacher, guide).
Stagnation: boredom, interpersonal impoverishment, pseudo-intimacy; resembles Jung's midlife crisis.
Basic strength: care, a broad concern for others shown in the need to teach.

sections.heading: Ego Integrity versus Despair
sections.detailed:
In the final stage, maturity and old age (55 and over), we face a choice between ego integrity and despair. These attitudes govern how we evaluate our whole life. Our main endeavours are complete or nearly so, and we reflect on life and take its final measure.

If we look back with fulfilment and satisfaction, believing we have coped with both victories and failures, we have ego integrity. Simply put, ego integrity means accepting one's place and one's past. If instead we review life with frustration, angry at missed opportunities and regretting mistakes that cannot be fixed, we feel despair: disgust with ourselves, contempt for others and bitterness over what might have been.

Erikson's own final stage. At 84 Erikson reported a long-term study of 29 people in their 80s for whom life-history data had been collected since 1928. The book's title, Vital Involvement in Old Age (Erikson, Erikson & Kivnick, 1986), states his prescription for ego integrity. Older people must do more than reflect; they must stay active, vital participants in life, seeking challenge and stimulation, for example through grandparenting, returning to school and developing new skills and interests. As an old man himself Erikson concluded that generativity was even more important than he had first thought: he said that much of the despair of older people is really a continuing sense of stagnation (quoted in Cheng, 2009). Generativity in the seventh stage may be the most important contributor to ego integrity in the eighth.

Wisdom. The basic strength of this final stage is wisdom. Arising from ego integrity, it is expressed as a detached concern with the whole of life and is passed to later generations as an integration of experience best described as heritage.

Maldevelopment (Table 6.2): excessive ego integrity leads to presumption; excessive despair leads to disdain.
sections.simple: After 55 we look back on our lives. Accepting our past with satisfaction is ego integrity; bitter regret over missed chances is despair. Erikson later said staying actively involved, and having been generative, is the key to integrity. The strength here is wisdom.
keyPoints: Maturity and old age, 55+; evaluating one's whole life.
Ego integrity = accepting one's place and past; despair = regret, self-disgust, bitterness.
Vital Involvement in Old Age (1986): study of 29 people in their 80s; prescription is staying active.
Erikson later saw generativity as the key contributor to ego integrity; despair is continued stagnation.
Basic strength: wisdom, a detached concern with life passed on as heritage.

sections.heading: Basic Weaknesses: Maladaptive and Malignant Conditions
sections.detailed:
Just as basic strengths can arise at each stage, so can basic weaknesses: motivating characteristics that come from unsatisfactory resolution of a developmental crisis. Recall that the adaptive and maladaptive ways of coping are meant to be combined in the ego in a kind of creative balance, with the adaptive attitude dominant but some negative attitude present.

Maladaptive and malignant conditions. In unbalanced development the ego consists solely of one attitude, either the adaptive or the maladaptive. Erikson called this maldevelopment. Note the potentially confusing labels (a favourite exam trap):
- When only the positive, adaptive tendency is present, the condition is called maladaptive.
- When only the negative tendency is present, the condition is called malignant.
Maladaptions can lead to neuroses; malignancies can lead to psychoses.

Correction (Review Question 15). Erikson believed both conditions could be corrected through psychotherapy. Maladaptions, the less severe disturbances, can also be relieved by re-adaptation, helped by environmental changes, supportive social relationships, or successful adaptation at a later stage.

Table 6.2 lists the maldevelopmental tendencies (adaptive excess first, then malignant):
- Oral-sensory: trust → sensory maladjustment; mistrust → withdrawal.
- Muscular-anal: autonomy → shameless willfulness; doubt/shame → compulsion.
- Locomotor-genital: initiative → ruthlessness; guilt → inhibition.
- Latency: industriousness → narrow virtuosity; inferiority → inertia.
- Adolescence: identity cohesion → fanaticism; role confusion → repudiation.
- Young adulthood: intimacy → promiscuity; isolation → exclusivity.
- Adulthood: generativity → overextension; stagnation → rejectivity.
- Maturity and old age: ego integrity → presumption; despair → disdain.
sections.simple: If the ego holds only one side of a crisis instead of a balance, Erikson called it maldevelopment. Only the positive side is "maladaptive" (can lead to neurosis); only the negative side is "malignant" (can lead to psychosis). Both can be treated with therapy, and milder maladaptions can also be fixed by better circumstances or later success.
keyPoints: Basic weaknesses come from unsatisfactory resolution of a crisis.
Maldevelopment = ego consisting solely of one way of coping.
Only adaptive tendency = maladaptive (to neuroses); only negative = malignant (to psychoses).
Both treatable by psychotherapy; maladaptions also by re-adaptation (environment, support, later success).
Table 6.2 gives two tendencies per stage, e.g. fanaticism vs. repudiation in adolescence.

sections.heading: Questions about Human Nature
sections.detailed:
A theorist who describes basic human strengths offers an optimistic view of human nature, and Erikson's image is clearly optimistic. Not everyone attains hope, purpose, wisdom and the other virtues, but everyone has the potential; nothing in our nature prevents it. Nor are we bound to suffer conflict, anxiety and neurosis because of instinctual biological forces.

The optimism rests on the structure of the stages: each is centred on a crisis but offers the possibility of a positive outcome. We can resolve each crisis in a way that is adaptive and strengthening, and even if we fail at one stage and develop a maladaptive response or basic weakness, change is still possible later.

Free will versus determinism. Erikson believed we can consciously direct and shape our growth throughout life; we are not solely products of childhood. His theory is only partially deterministic. In the first four stages the experiences provided by parents, teachers, peers and opportunities are largely outside our control. In the last four stages we have more room for free will, though the attitudes and strengths formed earlier influence our choices. Childhood matters, but later events can counteract unfortunate early experiences.

Nature versus nurture. In general Erikson held that personality is affected more by learning and experience than by heredity; psychosocial experiences, not instinctual biological forces, are the greater determinant.

Ultimate goal. Our overriding goal is to develop a positive ego identity that incorporates all the basic strengths.

Contrast with Freud (Review Question 16): Freud's image was pessimistic, with personality fixed largely in early childhood by biological instincts and conflict. Erikson's is optimistic, life-long, partly free and mainly psychosocial.
sections.simple: Erikson was optimistic: everyone can develop the basic strengths, and failure at one stage can be fixed later. We have little control in childhood but more free will as adults, and learning and social experience matter more than heredity. The ultimate goal is a positive ego identity.
keyPoints: Optimistic: everyone has potential for all virtues; neurosis is not inevitable.
Each crisis can be resolved positively; failures can be corrected later.
Partially deterministic: little control in first four stages, more free will in last four.
Learning and experience outweigh heredity (psychosocial over biological).
Ultimate goal: a positive ego identity incorporating all basic strengths.

sections.heading: Assessment in Erikson's Theory: Approach and Play Therapy
sections.detailed:
Erikson accepted some of Freud's theory but differed sharply in assessment methods. He doubted the usefulness and even the safety of some Freudian techniques, starting with the couch. Having patients lie on a couch, he felt, could lead to sadistic exploitation, create an illusion of objectivity, overemphasise unconscious material and make the therapist impersonal and aloof. To foster a more personal relationship of equals, he preferred patient and therapist to sit facing one another in comfortable chairs.

He relied less on formal assessment techniques than Freud. He occasionally used free association but rarely analysed dreams, which he called wasteful and harmful. He believed techniques should be chosen and modified to fit the unique needs of each patient.

Play therapy. With emotionally disturbed children, and in research on normal children and adolescents, Erikson used play therapy. He offered a variety of toys and observed how children interacted with them. The form and intensity of play revealed aspects of personality that children might not express verbally because of limited verbal ability.

Overall, Erikson built his theory mainly from three sources of data: play therapy, anthropological studies (such as his work with the Sioux in South Dakota and American Indians in California) and psychohistorical analysis (Review Question 17).
sections.simple: Erikson rejected Freud's couch, preferring face-to-face chairs, and rarely used dream analysis, which he thought wasteful and harmful. He tailored methods to each patient. With children he used play therapy, watching how they played with toys to see what they could not put into words.
keyPoints: Rejected the couch: risk of exploitation, false objectivity, overemphasis on the unconscious, aloofness.
Therapist and patient sat face to face as equals.
Occasional free association; dream analysis called wasteful and harmful.
Play therapy reveals what children cannot express verbally.
Main data sources: play therapy, anthropological studies, psychohistorical analysis.

sections.heading: Psychohistorical Analysis
sections.detailed:
Erikson's most unusual assessment technique was psychohistorical analysis: the application of his life-span theory, together with psychoanalytic principles, to the study of historical figures. These analyses are essentially biographical studies. He used his framework to describe the crises and coping styles of important political, religious and literary figures such as Gandhi, Martin Luther and George Bernard Shaw.

His psychohistories typically centre on one significant crisis, an episode representing a major life theme that unites the person's past, present and future activities. He used what he called "disciplined subjectivity": adopting the subject's viewpoint as his own so as to assess life events through that person's eyes.

Psychohistorical analysis was later used in research too; for example, Peterson and Stewart's analysis of Vera Brittain's writings supported the sequence of identity, intimacy and generativity (see research on the psychosocial stages).
sections.simple: Psychohistory means applying Erikson's life-span theory and psychoanalysis to famous people's lives, like Gandhi, Martin Luther and George Bernard Shaw. He focused on one key crisis that tied the person's life together, and tried to see events through their eyes ("disciplined subjectivity").
keyPoints: Psychohistorical analysis = life-span theory plus psychoanalysis applied to historical figures.
Essentially biographical; subjects included Gandhi, Martin Luther and George Bernard Shaw.
Focus on a significant crisis uniting past, present and future.
Disciplined subjectivity: adopting the subject's own viewpoint.

sections.heading: Psychological Tests
sections.detailed:
Erikson himself did not use psychological tests, but several instruments were later developed from his ideas:

- The Ego-Identity Scale (Dignan, 1965) measures the development of ego identity in adolescence.
- The Ego Identity Process Questionnaire (Balistreri, Busch-Rossnagel & Geisinger, 1995), also for adolescents, has 32 items measuring the dimensions of exploration and commitment.
- The Loyola Generativity Scale (McAdams & de St. Aubin, 1992) is a 20-item self-report inventory measuring generativity versus stagnation in adulthood. Table 6.3 gives sample items, such as trying to pass on knowledge gained from experience, believing one has made a difference to others, having others come for advice, and keeping commitments; reverse items include feeling that others do not need one, or that nothing one has done will survive one's death.

Other instruments appear in the research: the Inventory of Psychosocial Development, assessing adaptive and maladaptive development in the first six stages (Constantinople, 1969), and the 64-item Cross Racial Identity Scale for Black identity development.
sections.simple: Erikson didn't use tests, but others built them from his theory: the Ego-Identity Scale and the 32-item Ego Identity Process Questionnaire for teens, and the 20-item Loyola Generativity Scale for adults.
keyPoints: Erikson did not use tests himself.
Ego-Identity Scale (Dignan, 1965): adolescent ego identity.
Ego Identity Process Questionnaire: 32 items, exploration and commitment.
Loyola Generativity Scale (McAdams & de St. Aubin, 1992): 20-item self-report, generativity vs. stagnation.

sections.heading: Research on Erikson's Theory: Case Studies and Play Constructions
sections.detailed:
Erikson's primary research method was the case study. Its weaknesses are familiar (case material is hard to duplicate and verify), but it can yield much useful information. Erikson argued that case histories provide insights into personality development and help resolve patients' problems.

Play constructions. Using play therapy for research, Erikson studied play constructions: structures children build from dolls, blocks and other toys, which are then analysed. In one study boys and girls aged 10 to 12 were asked to build a scene from an imaginary movie using dolls, toy animals, toy cars and wooden blocks. Girls tended to build static, peaceful scenes with low, enclosed structures, into which intruders (animal or male figures, never female) tried to force their way. Boys focused on exteriors, action and height, building tall towers with cars and people in motion (Figure 6.1).

As an orthodox Freudian, Erikson interpreted these results psychoanalytically: the spatial differences paralleled genital anatomy, the external, intrusive male organ versus internal female organs. So biology determined that girls build low enclosures and boys build towers. He was criticised for implying that women are victims of their anatomy, their personalities shaped by lacking a penis. Erikson admitted the differences could also come from sex-role training, in which girls are less oriented toward action, aggression and achievement (Review Question 18).

Gender preferences for toys. More than 50 years later, gender stereotyping in toys persists. Boys typically play with trucks, soldiers and guns; girls with dolls, jewellery and toy kitchen items. Among 2- to 4-year-olds, boys played more with a train than a doll and girls the reverse (Wong & Hines, 2014). College men liked a model fighter jet only when painted blue, not pink (Dinella, Devita & Weisgram, 2013). Ten- to eleven-year-olds choosing software picked "Pirates" (boys) versus "Princesses" (girls) (Joiner, 1998).

The role of parents. These preferences are still taught by some parents, who buy most young children's toys, praise gender-appropriate play and discourage cross-gender play. Martin (1999) described a boy who dropped a race car instantly when the driver's helmet fell off to reveal a woman. Fathers treat sons and daughters more stereotypically than mothers do, so they are the main teachers of gender-based play; they reward passive, compliant behaviour in girls and assertive, aggressive behaviour in boys (Quiery, 1998).
sections.simple: Erikson mostly used case studies. In his play-constructions study, girls built low, enclosed, peaceful scenes and boys built tall towers and action scenes; he blamed anatomy, but critics (and later Erikson himself) pointed to sex-role training. Kids still prefer gender-typed toys today, a pattern taught mostly by parents, especially fathers.
keyPoints: Main research method: the case study (hard to duplicate and verify, but insightful).
Play constructions, ages 10–12: girls built low enclosed static scenes; boys built tall towers and action.
Erikson's anatomical interpretation was criticised; he conceded sex-role training could explain it.
Gender-typed toy preferences persist (Wong & Hines; Dinella et al.; Joiner).
Parents, especially fathers, teach and reinforce gender-typed play (Quiery).

sections.heading: Research: Trust and Security
sections.detailed:
Erikson stressed that an early sense of trust is needed for later feelings of security and well-being, and this position has strong research support (for example Jacobson & Wille, 1986; Londerville & Main, 1981; Sroufe, Fox & Pancake, 1983).

Infants aged 12 to 18 months with a strong emotional bond to their mothers (presumed high in trust) functioned at a higher social and emotional level when observed three years later than infants with less secure attachments. Children with well-developed trust were also more curious, sociable and popular, more often leaders at games, and more sensitive to others' needs and feelings. Those low in trust were more socially and emotionally withdrawn, reluctant to play with other children, less curious and less forceful in pursuing goals.

Holocaust survivors. Survivors interviewed 30 to 40 years after World War II had successfully dealt with all of Erikson's stages except the first: their view of others showed significantly more mistrust than trust (Suedfeld et al., 2005). Yet their success with later crises confirms Erikson's idea that positive events at later stages can counteract negative early experiences.
sections.simple: Research backs Erikson on trust: securely attached babies later did better socially and emotionally, and were more curious, popular and caring. Holocaust survivors were high in mistrust but still coped with later stages, showing later experiences can make up for early damage.
keyPoints: Early trust predicts later security and well-being (strong research support).
Securely attached infants (12–18 months) functioned better socially and emotionally 3 years later.
High-trust children: curious, sociable, popular, leaders, sensitive to others.
Holocaust survivors: mistrust dominated, yet later stages were resolved (Suedfeld et al., 2005).

sections.heading: Research: The Psychosocial Stages
sections.detailed:
Several studies support the sequence and themes of the stages.

Children's stories. Children aged 4, 8 and 11 made up stories about test pictures; the stories reflected Erikson's stage themes. Four-year-olds' stories concerned autonomy, the stage just completed, and older children's stories matched their own stages (Ciaccio, 1971).

Vera Brittain. A psychohistorical analysis of the diaries, letters and novels of the British feminist writer Vera Brittain (1893–1970), from age 21 into middle age, showed an early concern with ego identity shifting to intimacy and then generativity, exactly as predicted (Peterson & Stewart, 1990).

Adaptive and maladaptive development. Using the Inventory of Psychosocial Development, which assesses adaptive and maladaptive development in the first six stages, Constantinople (1969) found a significant link between happiness and adaptive development at each stage. Reimanis (1974) found a high correlation between maladaptive development in the first six stages and a sense of alienation and uprootedness. A Canadian study of 18- to 25-year-olds found emerging adulthood to be a period of increased psychological well-being (Galambos, Barker & Krahn, 2006).

The effects of growing up. Waterman, Buebel and Waterman (1970) tested whether resolving the identity crisis depends on earlier outcomes. Adolescents who had developed trust, autonomy, initiative and industriousness showed high identity cohesion; those with role confusion had not developed adaptive coping earlier. Among three groups of Canadian men (19–25, 35–55, 65–87), the youngest had the highest distress and the oldest the lowest, consistent with the idea that older people cope better after resolving earlier dilemmas (Beaumont & Zukanovic, 2005). British adults aged 62 to 89 recalling their past remembered trust, autonomy, initiative and industry issues from their first decade, identity issues from ages 11–20, and intimacy from young adulthood (Conway & Holmes, 2004).
sections.simple: Studies of children's stories, a famous writer's diaries, personality inventories and older people's memories all match Erikson's sequence of stages. Success at earlier stages predicts a firmer identity in adolescence, and older men reported less distress than younger men.
keyPoints: Children's stories reflected their stage themes (Ciaccio, 1971).
Vera Brittain's writings moved from identity to intimacy to generativity (Peterson & Stewart, 1990).
Adaptive development linked to happiness; maladaptive to alienation (Constantinople; Reimanis).
Earlier adaptive coping predicts identity cohesion (Waterman et al., 1970).
Older men less distressed (Beaumont & Zukanovic); memories follow stage themes (Conway & Holmes).

sections.heading: Research: Adolescent Development (Identity Statuses)
sections.detailed:
Marcia's extensive research programme (1966, 1980) identified five psychosocial types or statuses in adolescence: identity achievement, moratorium, foreclosure, identity diffusion and alienated achievement.

Identity achievement: adolescents committed to occupational and ideological choices. Achieved status correlated with objective measures of commitment (Streitmatter, 1993). These students had strong ego identity, were stable, had realistic goals, coped with change, did better on difficult tasks than role-confused peers, and chose harder majors such as engineering and the physical sciences (Marcia & Friedman, 1970). Teens reaching this status earlier were more likely to have stable romantic relationships in their twenties (Beyers & Seiffge-Krenke, 2010) and less likely to binge drink, use illegal drugs or take sexual risks (Schwartz et al., 2010). Studies of American, Chinese and Turkish students linked it to self-esteem, positive coping, well-being and a stronger self; it is the most psychologically and socially mature status. A programme of more than 120 studies found it rises over late adolescence and young adulthood (Kroger, Martinussen & Marcia, 2010). Parents of such adolescents gave direction and control in a loving way rather than being too permissive or too authoritarian (Berzonsky, 2004), a finding repeated with Iranian college students (Mohammadi, 2013).

Moratorium: people still in the identity crisis, with vague commitments and ambivalence toward authority (alternately rebelling and needing guidance). Their behaviour ranges from indecisive to active and creative; they score high in anxiety, and tend to daydream, believe in the supernatural and enjoy acting childishly (Bilsker & Marcia, 1991).

Foreclosure: adolescents who have not experienced a crisis but are committed to an occupation and ideology chosen for them by their parents. They tend to be rigid and authoritarian, struggle with change (Marcia, 1967), and are achievement-oriented toward external rather than internal goals (Stephen, Fraser & Marcia, 1992).

Identity diffusion: no occupational or ideological commitment and perhaps no crisis; in extreme cases aimless drifting, as Erikson did. They see their parents as indifferent and rejecting (Waterman, 1982). In Greece, Belgium and the US they showed poorer adjustment and well-being, unstable self-image and relationships, impulsive and self-destructive behaviour, excessive need for attention and grandiose fantasies.

Alienated achievement: adolescents who have had a crisis, have no occupational goal and hold beliefs critical of the social and economic system, which rules out careers within it. As students they are cerebral, philosophical and cynical.

Achieving an integrated ego identity. Four statuses in the order diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium, achievement represent increasingly successful resolution. Erikson's prediction that people with integrated identity have greater ego strength was supported in college men (Bourne, 1978). Extracurricular and volunteer activity was linked to higher fidelity (Markstrom et al., 2005), and more sport and exercise to stronger ego identity in Japanese and American students.
sections.simple: Marcia found five identity statuses in teens: achievement (committed after exploring), moratorium (still exploring), foreclosure (committed to parents' choices without exploring), diffusion (no commitment, drifting) and alienated achievement (rejecting the system). Identity achievement is the healthiest and is linked to loving but firm parents.
keyPoints: Marcia's five statuses: achievement, moratorium, foreclosure, diffusion, alienated achievement.
Identity achievement: committed, stable, high self-esteem, most mature; loving-but-directive parents.
Moratorium: still in crisis, anxious, ambivalent toward authority.
Foreclosure: commitments set by parents; rigid, authoritarian. Diffusion: no commitment, drifting.
Order diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium, achievement = increasingly successful resolution (Bourne).
Activities, volunteering and sports strengthen ego identity and fidelity.

sections.heading: Research: Sex Differences in Ego Identity and Adolescent Stress
sections.detailed:
Sex differences appear in how the identity crisis is resolved. Men in one study tended toward separation and detachment from others, women toward connection and attachment (Mellor, 1989). Other work extends this: male identity centres on individual competence and knowledge, female identity on relating to others. Women thus depend heavily on social relationships in forming identity, while men focus more on self and individual skills (Curry, 1998). Dutch data suggest females form an identity earlier than males, although most males achieve some identity by the end of the teens (Klimstra et al., 2010).

A stressful time to search for identity. Three key elements of adolescence have been identified: conflict with parents (forceful resistance to adult authority); mood disruption (volatile emotions, mood swings, depression); and risky behaviours (reckless, rule-breaking, antisocial acts that may harm self and others). In a diary study, 155 adolescents found that 31 percent of their daily interactions over two weeks involved conflict, and conflicts with parents were more important and emotionally intense than conflicts with peers (Jensen-Campbell & Graziano, 2000). Longitudinal studies found that many teens with depression and emotional problems had also shown distress as children, so adolescent difficulties do not necessarily arise because of adolescence (Steinberg & Morris, 2001).
sections.simple: Boys tend to build identity around their own skills and independence; girls around relationships, and girls may form an identity earlier. Adolescence often involves conflict with parents, mood swings and risky behaviour, but many troubled teens were already struggling as children.
keyPoints: Men: separation, detachment, individual competence; women: connection, relationships (Mellor; Curry).
Dutch females formed identity earlier than males (Klimstra et al., 2010).
Three elements of adolescent stress: parent conflict, mood disruption, risky behaviour.
31% of teens' interactions involved conflict; parent conflicts more intense (Jensen-Campbell & Graziano).
Teen problems often began in childhood (Steinberg & Morris, 2001).

sections.heading: Research: Virtual Identity
sections.detailed:
Computer games and social media let adolescents do exactly what Erikson said this stage requires: try different roles to find the best fit. Role-playing games such as Second Life and Dungeons and Dragons let young people adopt fictional personas and act out complex fantasies. Virtual places shared simultaneously by many users are called multi-user dungeons (MUDs); players interact with others and build personal virtual worlds.

Building a persona online. Players can be as like or unlike their real selves as they choose without revealing their real identity; Turkle noted you can completely redefine yourself, which is just what Erikson urged adolescents to do. German MUD players (average age 25) showed rising interpersonal attraction and social identification with the virtual community the longer they played (Utz, 2003), and identification with a virtual world may be as intense and satisfying as with the real one (Calvert et al., 2009). Second Life users seem to bring portions of their real, offline lives into their online self-presentation rather than inventing wholly fictional personas (Linares et al., 2011).

Advantages and disadvantages. Disclosing too much personal information online can prolong adolescence and delay a sound ego identity (Jordan-Conde et al., 2014). Seventh to ninth graders without a clear sense of their true self used social media more than those with a stronger identity (Israelashvili, Kim & Bukobza, 2012), raising the risk that a virtual identity could replace the developing true self (which can also happen offline). Australian children and adolescents high in loneliness and social anxiety were far more likely to discuss personal and intimate matters online (Bonetti, Campbell & Gilmore, 2010). On the positive side, personal home pages help identity formation: children who create them feel strong mastery and can express who they are more comfortably than face to face (Schmitt, Dayanim & Matthias, 2008). This section answers Review Question 21.
sections.simple: Online games and social media let teens try on different identities, exactly what Erikson said adolescents need. Virtual identities can feel as real as offline ones, and personal web pages can help, but oversharing or getting lost in an online persona can delay a real identity. Lonely, anxious teens use online sharing more.
keyPoints: Online role-play (Second Life, Dungeons and Dragons, MUDs) lets teens experiment with roles.
Identification with virtual communities grows over time and can be as satisfying as real ones.
Second Life users project parts of their real lives online.
Risks: oversharing delays identity; weak sense of self predicts heavy social media use.
Lonely, socially anxious youth share more intimately online; home pages can aid identity.

sections.heading: Research: Gender and Ego Identity
sections.detailed:
Effects of social forces over time. Erikson held that social and historical factors affect ego identity. The women's movement of the 1960s and 1970s served as a natural laboratory: were women who were adolescents then more affected than older women whose identities were already formed? Two major studies of women who graduated from college between the 1940s and mid-1960s said yes. Women in college when the movement began had greater aspirations, valued independence more, reached higher education, job status and income, and were more assertive and self-confident in middle age (Duncan & Agronick, 1995; Helson, Stewart & Ostrove, 1995).

Effects of a career orientation. More adolescent women came to include a career orientation in their identity, affecting dating and marriage age. Questionnaire studies found career-oriented college women married later, dated less and were warier of commitment. The reverse held for men: the stronger their career identity, the more committed they were to a dating relationship, and they avoided dating until committed to an occupation.

Differences in emotional life over time. A longitudinal study of women who graduated in the 1960s and their husbands measured positive emotionality (PEM: active, happy involvement in work and social life) and negative emotionality (NEM: stress, anxiety, anger) from the late 20s to mid-50s. Women scored higher than husbands on NEM in young adulthood and higher on PEM in late middle age, showing more social power, accomplishment and breadth of interest, and less stress and alienation, after child rearing ended. Social factors influence the emotional side of ego identity (Helson & Klohnen, 1998).

Adjustment to changing demands. Erikson defined identity consolidation as dealing successfully with the social realities of adult life, usually in the 20s as people take on marriage, family and career. Women graduates assessed at 21 and 27 who were high in ego resiliency and had found an identity in marriage were higher in identity consolidation (Pals, 1999). Among women aged 22 to 60, readiness to change was linked to changes in identity commitment, and contemplating change predicted exploring a new identity later (Anthis & LaVoie, 2006). Changed body image after breast cancer surgery triggered a hard-to-resolve identity crisis (Piot-Ziegler et al., 2010).

The identity crisis. Erikson placed the crisis at about 12 to 18, but it can come later: up to 30 percent were still searching at 24 (Archer, 1982). College may delay resolution and prolong experimentation (Cote & Levine, 1988); employed young people reached ego identity earlier than students, who stayed longer in moratorium (Adams & Fitch, 1982). Identity construction may continue over the whole life span (McAdams, 2001). A large study in India found girls higher in ego identity than boys (Janarthanam & Gnanadevan, 2014).
sections.simple: The women's movement shaped the identities of women who were in college at the time, giving them higher aspirations and success. Career-minded women married later, women grew happier after child rearing, and many people are still forming their identity in their twenties, with college delaying it.
keyPoints: Women in college during the 1960s–70s women's movement had higher aspirations and achievements.
Career-oriented women dated less and married later; career-committed men were more committed daters.
Women's PEM rose and NEM fell after child rearing (Helson & Klohnen, 1998).
Identity consolidation: adjusting to adult social realities, usually in the 20s.
Identity crisis may last past 18 (30% still searching at 24); college prolongs moratorium.
Indian study: girls higher in ego identity than boys.

sections.heading: Research: Generativity
sections.detailed:
Antecedents of generativity. Midlife generativity is significantly related to warm, affectionate parenting in childhood (Franz, McClelland & Weinberger, 1991); both mother and father matter. High-generativity adults believe in the goodness and worth of human life and are happier and more satisfied (McAdams & de St. Aubin, 1992; Van de Water & McAdams, 1989). Asked for major life themes, high scorers on the Loyola Generativity Scale described early good fortune, sensitivity to others' suffering, a stable belief system and clear goals for self and society; low scorers mentioned none of these (McAdams et al., 1997). Writing about high, low and turning points, high scorers described redemption sequences (negative experiences turned positive), low scorers the reverse (McAdams et al., 2001). College students restudied 20 and 30 years later showed that most who were slow to reach ego identity caught up by middle age and reached generativity (Whitbourne, Sneed & Sayer, 2009).

Correlates. Generativity is positively correlated with power and intimacy motivation (McAdams, Ruetzel & Foley, 1986), the needs to feel close to others and strong in relation to them, and with nurturance (Van de Water & McAdams, 1989): all needed for teaching and mentoring.

Benefits. High-generativity people score higher on extraversion, self-esteem, conscientiousness, altruism, competence, dutifulness and openness; have more satisfying relationships, community attachment and emotional stability (McAdams, Hart & Maruna, 1998); and more successful marriages, work success, close friendships and altruism (Westermeyer, 2004). Generativity is strongly tied to well-being for both parents and childless adults, most strongly when satisfaction comes from job and career rather than parenting (Clark & Arnold, 2008; Rothrauff & Cooney, 2008).

Generativity in women. High-generativity women (tested 31 to 48) had better emotional well-being (Vandewater, Ostrove & Stewart, 1997). Women valuing social recognition and achievement had fuller identities and higher generativity in their 40s (Helson & Srivastava, 2001). Generativity was higher in women's 40s than 20s, as predicted, but, contrary to Erikson, stayed at that level into their 60s (Zucker, Ostrove & Stewart, 2002). Women high in generativity at 43 maintained it 10 years later and gave more care to aging parents, spouses and children (Peterson, 2002).

Effect of technology. In Hong Kong, older people who felt out of touch with technology, the Internet and social media showed a marked decrease in generativity; feeling obsolete and unvalued, they disengaged from generative goals (Cheng, 2009).
sections.simple: Generative adults usually had warm parents, tell "redemption" stories about their lives, and are happier, more extraverted, conscientious and caring, with better marriages and careers. In women generativity rises from the 20s to the 40s and stays high. Older people who feel left behind by technology lose generativity.
keyPoints: Antecedent: warm, affectionate parenting in childhood.
High scorers tell redemption stories and have clear goals and stable beliefs (McAdams).
Correlates: power and intimacy motivation, nurturance.
Benefits: extraversion, self-esteem, conscientiousness, better marriages, careers and friendships.
Women: generativity higher in 40s than 20s but stable into 60s (contrary to Erikson).
Feeling obsolete with technology reduces generativity in older people (Cheng, 2009).

sections.heading: Research: Maturity
sections.detailed:
Reflecting on our lives. Erikson held that people in old age recall and examine their lives, accepting or regretting choices. Older psychologists' memories centred on college and early adult years, when the most critical decisions were made (Mackavey, Malley & Stewart, 1991). Elderly people high in ego integrity spent much more time reviewing their lives to resolve troubling issues than those low in integrity (Taft & Nehrke, 1990). In Portugal, reminiscing among over-65s produced ego integrity and well-being (Alfonso et al., 2011). Adults in their 50s and 60s who acknowledged regrets and missed opportunities had greater life satisfaction and physical health (Torges et al., 2005, 2008). People aged 60 to 69 showed heightened awareness of mortality, downsized goals and, for many, a continuing struggle with ego integrity (Robinson & Stell, 2014).

Concern with ego integrity. Belgian adults in their 60s and 70s who achieved ego integrity had higher subjective well-being, better psychological health, less fear of death and less bitterness (Van Hiel & Vansteenkiste, 2009). Across ages 17 to 82, older people cared more about generativity and ego integrity and less about ego identity, and age correlated positively with well-being: older people were generally happier (Sheldon & Kasser, 2001). Australians aged 55 to 93 who stayed involved in family and community kept feeling generative into old age (Warburton et al., 2006). Younger (25–35) and older (60–85) adults reflected equally often but for different reasons: the young for self-insight and current problem solving, the old to evaluate their lives and reach ego integrity (Staudinger, 2001).

Gender differences in aging. Women may find dispassionate life review harder. Men in their 60s reported much higher identity, certainty, confidence and power than women (Miner-Rubino, Winter & Stewart, 2004). A societal double standard sees aging as worse for women and labels them old earlier (a 50-year-old actress is cast as a widow or grandmother while a male peer gets powerful roles). Women also live longer and so face more illness, bereavement, loss of support and reduced income, which may explain why their life reviews are often less positive and more likely to lead to despair than integrity (Rainey, 1998).
sections.simple: Older people with ego integrity spend time reviewing their lives, admit regrets, and feel happier with less fear of death. Older adults are often happier than younger ones, and staying involved keeps generativity alive. Women may find old age harder due to ageist double standards, longer lives and more losses.
keyPoints: Life review and reminiscence linked to ego integrity (Taft & Nehrke; Alfonso et al.).
Acknowledging regrets relates to life satisfaction and health (Torges et al.).
Ego integrity: higher well-being, less fear of death and bitterness (Van Hiel & Vansteenkiste).
Older people more concerned with generativity/integrity and happier (Sheldon & Kasser).
Young reflect for insight, old to evaluate life (Staudinger).
Women face a double standard and more losses; reviews more likely to end in despair (Rainey).

sections.heading: Research: Racial and Ethnic Identity
sections.detailed:
Erikson did not consider racial identity and its benefits, but research consistently shows the importance of developing and keeping a racial or ethnic identity for minority groups; denying it can be stressful (Franklin-Jackson & Carter, 2007).

Benefits. Many studies of Latino, Asian and Black teenagers in the US, Hong Kong and Canada link strong ethnic identity to psychological well-being, high self-esteem, strong social bonds, life satisfaction and academic motivation. Black adolescents high in racial identity had higher well-being, life satisfaction and self-esteem and fewer mental health problems such as anxiety and depression. Among Black, Asian and biracial teens self-esteem was highest for Blacks, lowest for Asians, with biracial teens in between (Bracey et al., 2004), suggesting racial identity matters more for Black adolescents' self-esteem. Group esteem rose in African-American and Latino-American teens during early and middle adolescence while White students' stayed stable and high (French et al., 2006). Black adolescents high in ethnic identity had more negative attitudes to drugs and more positive attitudes to school, but those high in anti-White attitudes were more likely to use drugs and misbehave (Resnicow et al., 1999). More experienced racism meant more stress and poorer functioning (Bynum, Burton & Best, 2007). Gender identity also grows in importance with age; Black adolescents high in both racial and gender identity had better mental health and school adjustment (Rogers, 2013). Mexican-born US teens with a more traditionally Latino appearance had higher racial identity (Santos & Updegraff, 2014).

Women and racial identity. Among Black and Hispanic women, identity confusion (conflict between minority and majority culture) may lead to eating disorders such as anorexia through identification with the White majority's ideal of extreme thinness (Harris & Kuba, 1997).

Racial identity and ego identity. Ethnicity is central to ego identity in Asian-American and Hispanic-American adolescents; strong ethnic identity goes with high self-esteem and better peer and family relations (Phinney & Chavira, 1992). Hispanic-American teens in predominantly White schools had higher ethnic identity than those in balanced schools (Umana-Taylor, 2004). Strong Latino ethnic identity buffers stress and boosts well-being and achievement. Young Asian Americans with high ethnic identity resisted alcohol and marijuana more than more assimilated peers (Suinn, 1999), as did young Hispanics in immigrant families. Canadian First Nation adolescents identifying strongly with their own culture had stronger identity than those who saw themselves as bicultural (Gfellner & Armstrong, 2012).

Stages of developing racial identity. William Cross's Revised Racial Identity Model for African-American adolescents, measured by the 64-item Cross Racial Identity Scale (shown to be valid), has four stages:
1. Pre-encounter, with three clusters: assimilation (little racial awareness), miseducation (internalised negative stereotypes about Blacks) and self-hatred (anti-Black, self-hating attitudes).
2. Encounter: experiencing racism or discrimination shifts the worldview.
3. Immersion-emersion, with two identities: intense Black involvement (everything Black is good) and anti-White (everything White is evil).
4. Internalization, with two identities: Black nationalism (pro-Black Afrocentric) and multiculturalist inclusive (embracing Black and other ethnic, racial and gender identities).
Black men in the pre-encounter stage had lower self-esteem and well-being and more distress than those in internalization (Pierre & Mahalik, 2005), and Black college students' defence mechanisms matured as their racial identity advanced (Nghe & Mahalik, 2001). The model's importance is in treating ethnic identity as a vital part of ego identity that develops in stages, just like Erikson's (Review Question 20).
sections.simple: Erikson ignored race, but research shows a strong ethnic identity helps minority teens: better self-esteem, well-being, school attitudes and less drug use. Cross's model says healthy Black identity develops through four stages: pre-encounter, encounter, immersion-emersion and internalization.
keyPoints: Not considered by Erikson; strong ethnic identity linked to well-being, self-esteem, school motivation.
Black teens: racial identity strongly tied to self-esteem; anti-White attitudes linked to problems.
Ethnic identity buffers stress and protects against substance use.
Identity confusion with White beauty ideals may lead to eating disorders (Harris & Kuba).
Cross model: pre-encounter, encounter, immersion-emersion, internalization (64-item scale).
Advanced stages bring better well-being and more mature defences.

sections.heading: Research: Gender Preference Identity
sections.detailed:
Gender preference identity is another aspect of ego identity Erikson did not directly consider. It may affect overall ego identity and vary with ethnic identity: among White, Black and Hispanic children (average age 11), Black and Hispanic children reported much more pressure for gender conformity (Corby, Hodges & Perry, 2007).

Stages of identity. Researchers propose that LGBT identity develops in stages, like Erikson's ego identity or ethnic identity. Frable's (1997) model has four stages (Review Question 24):
1. Sensitization: before adolescence, an initial sense of being different from same-sex peers.
2. Identity confusion: in adolescence, the confusing, perhaps frightening, realisation that one's feelings and thoughts could be described as homosexual.
3. Identity assumption: the person comes to believe he or she is homosexual and begins to accept a gay identity.
4. Commitment: full acceptance of the gay identity as a way of life.

Consequences. Despite greater acceptance, people with transgender and other nontraditional gender preference identities face significant challenges: higher stress, depression, suicide, failure and guilt, and physical and mental health problems. They suffer bullying, harassment and discrimination, especially at school, affecting well-being and grades; seeing other students intervene softens the impact and encourages intervention, and strong family and friend support greatly reduces harm (Wernick, Kulick & Inglehart, 2014). Coming out and expressing pride without wishing to change or hide one's identity is linked to better mental and emotional well-being (Bockting, 2014), higher self-esteem and lower depression (Frable, 1997; Kosciw et al., 2014). Among male prison inmates, those with a strong need for personal relationships had less gender role conflict, the need for others perhaps overriding homophobia; those with less need for contact had more conflict about homosexual tendencies (Schwartz et al., 2004).
sections.simple: Erikson didn't address sexual identity, but researchers say it also develops in stages: sensitization, identity confusion, identity assumption and commitment (Frable). People with nontraditional identities face more stress and harassment, but support and coming out with pride are linked to better well-being.
