keyPoints: Not directly considered by Erikson; varies with ethnic identity (Corby et al.).
Frable's four stages: sensitization, identity confusion, identity assumption, commitment.
Nontraditional identities linked to more stress, depression and health problems.
Peer intervention and social support reduce the harm of harassment.
Coming out with pride relates to higher self-esteem and lower depression.

sections.heading: Reflections: Contributions and Criticisms
sections.detailed:
Contributions. Erikson's major contributions are the recognition that personality develops throughout the life span, the concept of the adolescent identity crisis, and the incorporation of cultural, social and historical forces into personality theory.

Criticisms (Review Question 25).
1. Ambiguity and imprecision: critics point to ambiguous terms and concepts, conclusions without supporting data and an overall lack of precision (Rosenthal, Gurney & Moore, 1981; Waterman, 1982). Erikson accepted these charges, blaming his artistic temperament and lack of formal scientific training; he wrote that, coming to psychology from art, he sometimes painted contexts where readers wanted facts.
2. Incomplete description of maturity, which he tried to remedy in Vital Involvement in Old Age (1986). Some also doubt that development after 55 is as positive as ego integrity implies; for many it brings pain, loss and depression even with wisdom.
3. Sex differences: his anatomical interpretation of the play-constructions research is attacked, since the differences could be cultural or due to sex-role training, which Erikson later admitted.
4. Applicability to women: Carol Tavris found she was not having her crises in the right order, with identity still shaky after adolescence and intimacy and generativity on hold because she had not married on schedule.
5. Social class: the theory may not apply to people in reduced economic circumstances who cannot afford an adolescent moratorium; it may be a luxury for those who can attend college or travel, as Erikson did for seven years (Slugoski & Ginsburg, 1989).

Erikson showed little interest in answering critics; he accepted that there are many ways to describe personality development and no single view is adequate. His influence spread through his books and through psychologists, psychiatrists, teachers and counsellors who found his ideas useful from infancy to old age.
sections.simple: Erikson's big contributions were life-span development, the identity crisis, and bringing culture and history into personality theory. Critics say his terms are vague and unsupported, his old-age stage is incomplete and too rosy, his views on sex differences are biased, and his stages may not fit women or poorer people.
keyPoints: Contributions: life-span development, adolescent identity crisis, cultural/social/historical forces.
Criticism: ambiguous terms, lack of data and precision (Erikson blamed his artistic background).
Maturity stage incomplete; old age may be less positive than ego integrity suggests.
Anatomical view of sex differences criticised; Tavris found the stages did not fit women.
Moratorium may be a luxury unavailable to poorer people (Slugoski & Ginsburg).

sections.heading: Reflections: Recognition and Influence
sections.detailed:
Erikson's ideas were recognised in both professional and popular circles. Time magazine called him the most influential living psychoanalyst (1975), and Psychology Today called him an authentic intellectual hero (Hall, 1983). His concepts are used in education, social work, vocational and marriage counselling, and clinical work with children and adolescents, and Clark (2010) notes that his work remains meaningful for contemporary psychology and social thought. The Erikson Institute for Early Childhood Education was set up for graduate training in 1966 at Chicago's Loyola University.

Life-span developmental psychology, which has grown massively in recent years, owes much of its spark to Erikson, as does the current interest in developmental problems of middle and old age. His play therapy has become a standard diagnostic and therapeutic tool for emotionally disturbed and abused children: children who cannot describe a physical or sexual attack in words can express their feelings through play, using dolls to represent themselves and their abusers.
sections.simple: Erikson was hugely recognised, called the most influential living psychoanalyst. His ideas are used in education, counselling and child therapy, sparked life-span developmental psychology, and his play therapy is now a standard way to help abused children express what happened.
keyPoints: Time: most influential living psychoanalyst; Psychology Today: an authentic intellectual hero.
Applied in education, social work, vocational and marriage counselling, child clinical work.
Erikson Institute for Early Childhood Education founded 1966 in Chicago.
Sparked life-span developmental psychology and interest in middle and old age.
Play therapy is a standard tool with disturbed and abused children.

Failure to achieve ego identity during adolescence, resulting in role confusion.
Erikson's early term for a lack of clear self-image caused by alienation from cultural traditions, seen in American Indians and WWII veterans.
Erikson's view of adolescence as a necessary pause between childhood and adulthood for experimenting with roles and self-images.
An identity society disapproves of (e.g., in crime or drugs), which Erikson considered better than no identity at all.

A condition in which the ego consists solely of one way of coping with conflict, either adaptive or maladaptive.

Accepting one's place and one's past with fulfilment when reviewing life in old age.
Marcia's status for adolescents committed to occupational and ideological choices; the most mature status.

Virtual places shared simultaneously by many computer users, where players interact and build virtual worlds.
Active, happy involvement in one's work and social environments.
Feelings of stress, anxiety, anger and other negative emotions.
Erikson's term for dealing successfully with the social realities of adult life, usually in the 20s.
How people feel about being members of their racial or ethnic group.

studies.title: Erikson: play constructions (ages 10–12)
studies.finding: Girls built static, peaceful, low enclosed scenes intruded on by males/animals; boys built tall towers and action scenes. Erikson credited anatomy, later conceded sex-role training.

studies.title: Wong & Hines (2014): toy choice at 2–4
studies.finding: Boys played more with a train, girls with a doll.

studies.title: Dinella, Devita & Weisgram (2013): fighter jet colour
studies.finding: College men liked a model fighter jet only when blue, rejecting it when pink.

studies.title: Joiner (1998): software choice
studies.finding: Boys aged 10–11 chose 'Pirates' software, girls 'Princesses'.

studies.title: Martin (1999): race-car driver
studies.finding: A boy dropped a toy race car when the driver turned out to be a woman.

studies.title: Quiery (1998): fathers and gender roles
studies.finding: Fathers reward passive compliance in girls and assertiveness/aggression in boys, treating children more stereotypically than mothers.

studies.title: Attachment and trust (Sroufe et al.; Londerville & Main; Jacobson & Wille)
studies.finding: Securely attached infants (12–18 months) functioned better socially and emotionally 3 years later; high-trust children were curious, popular, leaders and sensitive.

studies.title: Suedfeld et al. (2005): Holocaust survivors
studies.finding: Resolved all stages except trust vs. mistrust (more mistrust), showing later stages can overcome early damage.

studies.title: Ciaccio (1971): children's stories
studies.finding: Stories of 4-, 8- and 11-year-olds reflected their stage themes; 4-year-olds wrote about autonomy.

studies.title: Peterson & Stewart (1990): Vera Brittain
studies.finding: Her concerns moved from identity to intimacy to generativity as predicted.

studies.title: Constantinople (1969): Inventory of Psychosocial Development
studies.finding: Adaptive development at each of the first six stages related to happiness.

studies.title: Reimanis (1974)
studies.finding: Maladaptive development in the first six stages correlated highly with alienation and uprootedness.

studies.title: Galambos, Barker & Krahn (2006)
studies.finding: Canadians aged 18–25: emerging adulthood brought increased psychological well-being.

studies.title: Waterman, Buebel & Waterman (1970)
studies.finding: Adolescents with trust, autonomy, initiative and industriousness showed identity cohesion; role-confused ones lacked earlier adaptive coping.

studies.title: Beaumont & Zukanovic (2005): Canadian men
studies.finding: Distress highest in men 19–25 and lowest in men 65–87.

studies.title: Conway & Holmes (2004): memories of older Britons
studies.finding: Memories from each decade centred on the matching stage issue (trust/autonomy/initiative/industry, then identity, then intimacy).

studies.title: Streitmatter (1993); Marcia & Friedman (1970)
studies.finding: Identity achievement correlated with commitment; achievers were stable, realistic, chose harder majors.

studies.title: Beyers & Seiffge-Krenke (2010); Schwartz et al. (2010)
studies.finding: Early identity achievers had stable romances in their twenties and less binge drinking, drug use and sexual risk.

studies.title: Kroger, Martinussen & Marcia (2010): 120+ studies
studies.finding: Identity achievement rose over late adolescence and young adulthood.

studies.title: Berzonsky (2004); Mohammadi (2013)
studies.finding: Identity achievers had loving, directive parents; too permissive or authoritarian parenting hindered achievement (also in Iran).

studies.finding: Foreclosed teens rigid, authoritarian, poor at change; achievement-oriented toward external goals.

studies.finding: Men's identity: separation and individual competence; women's: connection and relationships.

studies.finding: Children's personal home pages gave mastery and a comfortable way to express identity.

examples.title: Autonomy: a toddler insisting on 'I do it'
examples.text: A two-year-old insists on putting on her own sandals even though it takes ten minutes. A parent who waits patiently supports autonomy; one who snatches the sandals and scolds her for being slow risks building doubt and shame.

examples.title: Moratorium vs. foreclosure in an Indian family
examples.text: One student takes a gap year, tries design, coding and volunteering before choosing a field (moratorium heading toward identity achievement). His cousin enrolls in engineering because the family always planned it, without ever questioning it (foreclosure).

examples.title: Generativity at work
examples.text: A senior bank manager with no children spends Saturdays training new recruits and mentoring rural students for entrance exams. This is generativity: it is about guiding the next generation, not about being a parent.

examples.title: Ego integrity vs. despair at retirement
examples.text: Two retired teachers look back. One says she made mistakes but is proud of the students she shaped (integrity). The other keeps saying he wasted his life and blames everyone around him (despair).

examples.title: Maldevelopment: too much trust
examples.text: A person who trusts everyone completely shares bank details with a stranger on a call. Erikson would see sensory maladjustment: only the adaptive tendency, with no healthy mistrust to protect him.

checks.q: Which was NOT one of Erikson's three extensions of Freud?
options: Development continues over the whole life span
The ego is independent of the id
Cultural and historical forces shape personality

checks.q: How did Erikson view the ego relative to the id?
options: As an independent part of personality
checks.explain: He placed more emphasis on the ego and saw it as not dependent on the id, unlike Freud.

checks.q: Erikson kept the surname Homburger until he
checks.explain: He took the name Erik Homburger Erikson at 37 on becoming a U.S. citizen.

checks.q: Erikson first called the lack of clear self-image he saw in American Indians and WWII veterans
checks.explain: He initially called it identity confusion, caused by alienation from culture and traumatic uprooting.

options: genes determine the stages, while the environment governs how they are realised
the environment determines the order of the stages
crises are caused solely by biology
checks.explain: Inherited forces set the stages; social forces control how they are realised.

options: mainly adaptive but with some of the negative attitude

practice.q: What is the epigenetic principle of maturation?
practice.answer: The epigenetic principle of maturation is Erikson's idea that human development unfolds in a sequence of stages determined by inherited (genetic) factors; epi means 'upon', so development rests on genetic foundations. However, social and environmental forces control how each predetermined stage is actually realised, so personality reflects both biology and social experience.

Maldevelopment occurs when the ego holds only one way of coping. If only the positive, adaptive tendency is present (e.g., total trust, giving sensory maladjustment) it is maladaptive and can lead to neuroses. If only the negative tendency is present (e.g., total mistrust, giving withdrawal) it is malignant and can lead to psychoses. Both can be corrected through psychotherapy.

Psychohistorical analysis is Erikson's application of his life-span theory and psychoanalytic principles to historical figures such as Gandhi, Martin Luther and George Bernard Shaw. These biographical studies focus on a major crisis uniting past, present and future, and use 'disciplined subjectivity', viewing events through the subject's eyes.

practice.q: Name the stages of gender preference identity proposed by Frable.
practice.answer: Frable (1997) proposed four stages: (1) sensitization, a pre-adolescent sense of being different from same-sex peers; (2) identity confusion, the adolescent, often frightening realisation that one's feelings may be homosexual; (3) identity assumption, beginning to accept a gay identity; and (4) commitment, full acceptance of the gay identity as a way of life.

practice.q: Describe Erikson's own identity crises and explain how they were reflected in his theory.
practice.answer:
Erikson's life illustrates how a theory can grow from its author's experience. He was born in Frankfurt to a Danish mother who never revealed his father's identity. She married his pediatrician, Theodore Homburger, and Erik grew up unsure of his name and identity, using the name Homburger until he became a U.S. citizen at 37 and renamed himself Erikson. At school, German classmates rejected him as Jewish, while Jewish classmates rejected him for his Aryan appearance.

After high school he drifted through Europe as an artist, feeling neurotic and close to psychotic, repeatedly leaving art schools to continue searching for an identity. Only when he began teaching in Vienna and trained with Anna Freud did he feel he had found one. Even late in life, his daughter reports, he remained ashamed of his illegitimacy.

These experiences appear throughout his theory. The concept of the identity crisis, the psychological moratorium of adolescence, and the idea that one may withdraw from the normal life sequence (as he did) all mirror his own path. He even admitted that he needed to name the crisis and see it in everyone in order to deal with it himself. His later observations of identity confusion in uprooted American Indians and war veterans extended this personal theme into a general theory of ego identity.

practice.q: Explain the role of conflict and crisis in Erikson's psychosocial stages, and describe the two ways of responding to each crisis.
practice.answer:
For Erikson, development is a series of personal conflicts. Their potential is present at birth as innate predispositions, and each becomes prominent at a particular stage when the environment demands a new adaptation. Each such confrontation is a crisis, a turning point requiring a shift in perspective and a refocusing of energy to fit the needs of that stage.

Each crisis can be met in a maladaptive (negative) or an adaptive (positive) way, for example mistrust or trust in infancy. Only when a conflict is resolved can personality continue normally and gain strength for the next stage; an unresolved conflict makes later adaptation harder, though success remains possible.

Importantly, the ego should incorporate both ways of coping. Trust is healthier, but some mistrust protects us from deception and manipulation. The ideal resolution is an ego dominated by the adaptive attitude yet balanced by some of the negative one. A satisfactory resolution produces a basic strength such as hope; one-sided development, containing only one attitude, produces maldevelopment (maladaptive or malignant tendencies). Because the strengths are interdependent, each stage's resolution prepares the ground for the next crisis.

practice.q: Describe Marcia's five identity statuses and the research findings on each.
practice.answer:
Marcia identified five adolescent statuses. Identity achievement describes adolescents committed to occupational and ideological choices. They are stable, realistic, cope well with change, choose difficult majors, have high self-esteem and well-being, form stable romances in their twenties and avoid risky behaviour. Their parents gave loving direction rather than being too permissive or authoritarian.

Moratorium describes those still in the identity crisis, with vague commitments and ambivalence toward authority; they are anxious, may daydream and believe in the supernatural. Foreclosure describes adolescents committed to choices made by their parents without having had a crisis; they are rigid, authoritarian and struggle with change, pursuing external goals.

Identity diffusion describes those with no commitments and possibly no crisis, sometimes drifting aimlessly; they see parents as indifferent and show poor adjustment, unstable self-image and impulsivity. Alienated achievement describes those who had a crisis but reject the social and economic system and so avoid careers; they are cerebral and cynical.

Diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium and achievement represent increasingly successful resolution, and Bourne found greater ego strength in those with integrated identity. A review of more than 120 studies showed identity achievement rising over late adolescence and young adulthood, as Erikson predicted.

practice.q: How does Erikson's image of human nature differ from Freud's?
practice.answer:
Erikson's image is far more optimistic than Freud's. By describing basic strengths such as hope, purpose and wisdom, he implied that everyone has the potential to develop these virtues; nothing in human nature prevents it, and we are not doomed to conflict, anxiety and neurosis by biological instincts, as Freud's view suggested.

Each stage centres on a crisis but offers a positive outcome, and failure at one stage can be corrected later. Freud saw personality as largely fixed by the first five years; Erikson held that we can consciously direct our growth throughout life and that later events can counteract early misfortunes.

On free will versus determinism, Erikson is only partially deterministic: in the first four stages experiences are largely beyond our control, but in the last four we have more free will, though earlier outcomes shape our choices. On nature versus nurture, he emphasised learning and psychosocial experience over heredity, whereas Freud emphasised instinctual biological forces. Finally, Erikson's ultimate goal is a positive ego identity incorporating all basic strengths, reflecting his focus on an independent ego rather than the id. Thus, where Freud saw people as victims of biology and childhood, Erikson saw them as capable of growth at every stage.

practice.q: Describe the concept of generativity, give an example of how it can be achieved, and summarise research comparing people high and low in generativity.
practice.answer:
Generativity is the adaptive pole of the seventh stage (about 35–55). It is the need to be actively involved in teaching and guiding the next generation, a concern that extends beyond one's family to future society. Parenthood is neither necessary nor sufficient. All institutions offer outlets, so a person might mentor junior colleagues, teach, or guide young people through social service. Failure leads to stagnation, boredom and self-absorption; success yields care.

Research shows that generativity is rooted in warm childhood parenting. High scorers on the Loyola Generativity Scale believe in the worth of human life, are happier and more satisfied, report life themes of early good fortune, sensitivity to suffering and clear goals, and tell redemption stories. They score higher in extraversion, self-esteem, conscientiousness, altruism and openness, have more satisfying relationships, successful marriages and careers, and greater well-being, whether or not they are parents. Generativity correlates with power and intimacy motivation and nurturance. Low scorers lack these themes and tell stories where good events turn bad. Most people slow to reach ego identity still catch up and become generative by midlife (Whitbourne et al.), while older people who feel out of touch with technology lose generativity (Cheng).

practice.q: Describe the eight psychosocial stages of Erikson's theory with their ages, crises and basic strengths. What is the major difference between the first four and the last four stages?
practice.answer:
Introduction
Erik Erikson extended Freud's theory by proposing that personality develops across the whole life span in eight psychosocial stages. Governed by the epigenetic principle, the stages are genetically ordered but realised through social experience. Each involves a crisis with an adaptive and a maladaptive way of coping; a balanced, mainly adaptive resolution yields a basic strength.

The four childhood stages
1. Oral-sensory (birth–1): trust vs. mistrust. The helpless infant depends on the mother; consistent love and care produce trust and the start of ego identity, while rejection or inconsistency produces mistrust. Strength: hope.
2. Muscular-anal (1–3): autonomy vs. doubt and shame. Toddlers exercise choice for the first time; holding on and letting go are prototypes for later behaviour. Forced toilet training breeds doubt and shame. Strength: will.
3. Locomotor-genital (3–5): initiative vs. guilt. Children take initiative, including Oedipal fantasies; punishment creates lasting guilt, loving guidance channels initiative into socially approved goals (the superego). Strength: purpose.
4. Latency (6–11): industriousness vs. inferiority. At school children develop work habits and skills; praise fosters competence, ridicule fosters inferiority. Strength: competence.

The four later stages
5. Adolescence (12–18): identity cohesion vs. role confusion. In a psychological moratorium adolescents experiment with roles to form ego identity; failure, the identity crisis, causes role confusion or a negative identity. Strength: fidelity.
6. Young adulthood (18–35): intimacy vs. isolation. Caring, committed relationships merge identities without losing them; failure brings isolation. Strength: love, the greatest virtue.
7. Adulthood (35–55): generativity vs. stagnation. Adults guide the next generation through family, work or institutions; failure brings stagnation, boredom and pseudo-intimacy. Strength: care.
8. Maturity and old age (55+): ego integrity vs. despair. Reviewing life with acceptance gives integrity; regret and bitterness give despair. Erikson later stressed staying vitally involved and saw generativity as key. Strength: wisdom.

First four versus last four
The outcome of the first four stages depends mainly on other people: it is more a function of what is done to children by parents and teachers than of what they do themselves. In the last four stages we gain increasing conscious control, choosing friends, colleges, careers, spouses and leisure. Still, whether the ego emerges from childhood mainly with trust, autonomy, initiative and industriousness, or with mistrust, doubt, guilt and inferiority, strongly shapes these choices.

Conclusion
Erikson's stages give an optimistic, life-long picture in which each crisis offers a chance for growth and earlier failures can be repaired later, a major broadening of Freud's childhood-centred model. The basic strengths are interdependent, each depending on confirmation of the previous one, and a healthy ego retains some of the negative pole (a little mistrust, for instance) as protection. One-sided development produces maldevelopment, such as fanaticism or repudiation in adolescence. Research supports the sequence: children's stories reflect their current stage themes (Ciaccio), Vera Brittain's writings moved from identity to intimacy to generativity, and older adults' memories of each decade centre on the matching stage issue.

practice.q: Critically evaluate Erikson's theory, discussing his assessment methods, research support, contributions and criticisms.
practice.answer:
Introduction
Erikson's identity theory remains one of the most influential personality theories. Evaluating it requires looking at how he gathered data, how far research supports it, and what its strengths and weaknesses are.

Assessment methods
Erikson differed from Freud in assessment. He rejected the couch as potentially exploitative and impersonal, preferring face-to-face chairs, used free association only occasionally and considered dream analysis wasteful and harmful. He tailored techniques to each patient. His main data sources were play therapy, in which children's play revealed what they could not verbalise; anthropological studies such as his work on Sioux child-rearing; and psychohistorical analysis of figures like Gandhi and Martin Luther using disciplined subjectivity. Later researchers built tests from his ideas, including the Ego-Identity Scale, the Ego Identity Process Questionnaire and the Loyola Generativity Scale. His own research relied on case studies, which are hard to duplicate and verify, though he argued they yield rich insights into development and help resolve patients' problems.

Research support
Support is considerable, particularly for the first six stages and ego identity. Early secure attachment predicts later social competence; Holocaust survivors high in mistrust still mastered later stages, confirming that later events can repair early damage. Children's stories, Vera Brittain's writings and older adults' memories follow the predicted stage themes. Adaptive earlier development predicts identity cohesion. Marcia's statuses show identity achievement to be the most mature outcome. Generativity is linked to happiness, better relationships and well-being, and ego integrity to less fear of death. However, research also shows the identity crisis may extend into the twenties, college can prolong moratorium, and women's generativity does not decline as predicted.

Contributions
Erikson showed that personality develops over the entire life span, introduced the adolescent identity crisis, and incorporated cultural, social and historical forces. Research on virtual, ethnic and gender preference identity extends his framework. He sparked life-span developmental psychology, his ideas are used in education, counselling and social work, and play therapy is now standard with abused children.

Criticisms
Critics cite ambiguous concepts, conclusions lacking data and imprecision, which Erikson blamed on his artistic background. The maturity stage was incompletely described and may be too positive given the pain and loss of old age. His anatomical reading of play constructions is seen as biased; sex-role training is an alternative he later accepted. Tavris argued the stages do not fit women's lives, and Slugoski and Ginsburg argued the moratorium is a luxury unavailable to poorer people. He also neglected racial and ethnic identity, now shown to be central for minority youth.

Conclusion
Despite vagueness and cultural bias, Erikson's theory has strong research support and enormous practical influence, which explains why he was called the most influential living psychoanalyst. On balance, his theory is better at describing and organising development than at producing precise, testable predictions, but its broad life-span framework has generated decades of productive research, from Marcia's identity statuses to McAdams's work on generativity, and continues to be extended to new areas such as online identity and minority identity development.

practice.q: Discuss research on ego identity in adolescence, including virtual identity, sex differences and racial and ethnic identity.
practice.answer:
Introduction
Erikson saw adolescence (12–18) as the stage of ego identity versus role confusion, a moratorium for experimenting with roles. A large body of research tests and extends this idea.

Identity statuses
Marcia identified five statuses. Identity achievement (commitment after exploration) is the most mature, associated with stability, realistic goals, high self-esteem, stable later romances and less risky behaviour, and is fostered by loving but directive parents. Moratorium involves ongoing crisis and anxiety; foreclosure involves commitments adopted from parents, rigidity and authoritarianism; identity diffusion involves no commitment, poor adjustment and impulsivity; alienated achievement involves rejection of the social system. Diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium and achievement represent increasingly successful resolutions, and integrated identity brings greater ego strength. Extracurricular activities, volunteering and sport strengthen identity and fidelity.

Timing and stress
The crisis may extend into the twenties: up to 30 percent were still searching at 24, and college students stay in moratorium longer than employed peers. Adolescence involves conflict with parents, mood disruption and risky behaviour, though many troubled teens had difficulties in childhood too.

Sex differences
Male identity tends to centre on separation and individual competence, female identity on connection and relationships, and Dutch girls formed identity earlier than boys. Women's identity has been shaped by social forces such as the women's movement and career orientation: women in college when the movement began had higher aspirations and later achievement, and career-oriented women married later. This supports Erikson's emphasis on history and culture. An Indian study found girls higher in ego identity than boys.

Virtual identity
Online games, MUDs and social media allow exactly the role experimentation Erikson described. Identification with virtual communities can be as satisfying as offline identification, and users often project parts of their real lives online. Personal home pages aid mastery and self-expression, but oversharing can delay identity, and teens lacking a true sense of self, or who are lonely and anxious, rely more on online communication.

Racial and ethnic identity
Erikson did not consider race, but a strong ethnic identity among minority youth is linked to well-being, self-esteem, life satisfaction, academic motivation, resistance to drugs and buffering of stress, while identity confusion with majority beauty ideals may contribute to eating disorders. Cross's Revised Racial Identity Model describes four stages (pre-encounter, encounter, immersion-emersion, internalization); advanced stages bring better well-being and more mature defences.

Conclusion
Research broadly confirms the importance of ego identity in adolescence while showing that its timing, content and pathways vary with gender, culture, ethnicity and technology. These findings also extend Erikson's own position: he stressed culture and history in principle, but research on ethnic identity and gender preference identity (Frable's stages of sensitization, identity confusion, identity assumption and commitment) shows aspects of identity he did not directly consider, each developing in stages much like his psychosocial sequence.

practice.q: In what ways does Erikson's theory differ from Freud's?
practice.answer:
Erikson saw psychoanalysis as his starting point but departed from Freud in several ways. First, he extended development over the whole life span with eight stages, whereas Freud's stages end in childhood and adolescence. Second, he gave the ego greater emphasis and made it independent of the id rather than subservient to it. Third, he stressed cultural, social and historical forces; even in the stages that parallel Freud's oral, anal, phallic and latency periods, he emphasised psychosocial rather than biological correlates (for example, toilet training as a psychosocial conflict over autonomy).

His image of human nature is more optimistic: each crisis can be resolved positively, failures can be corrected later, and we can consciously shape our growth; Freud saw people as driven by instincts and largely fixed by early childhood. Erikson's theory is only partially deterministic and emphasises learning over heredity.

His methods also differed. He rejected the couch in favour of face-to-face seating as equals, rarely analysed dreams (calling it wasteful and harmful), and relied on play therapy, anthropological studies and psychohistorical analysis. He also studied normal people from diverse cultures, not just disturbed patients.

practice.q: What did Erikson mean by identity confusion, and what evidence did he find for it among American Indians and World War II veterans?
practice.answer:
Identity confusion is Erikson's original term for the lack of a clear self-image or self-identity, a confusion about who and what one is. It later developed into his concepts of the identity crisis and role confusion.

While observing American Indians in South Dakota (in a study of Sioux child-rearing with a Yale anthropologist) and in California, Erikson noticed psychological symptoms that orthodox Freudian theory could not explain. These seemed linked to a sense of alienation from cultural traditions, which left people without a clear self-image.

He saw a similar condition in emotionally disturbed veterans after World War II. He argued that these men were not suffering from repressed conflicts, as Freud would claim, but from confusion caused by traumatic war experiences and by being temporarily uprooted from their culture. In both groups, then, disruption of the person's cultural and social context undermined identity. This evidence reinforced Erikson's emphasis on culture and history and his view that identity problems are psychosocial rather than purely instinctual. It also echoed Erikson's own life: as a child rejected by both German and Jewish classmates and unsure of his name, he had experienced the same uncertainty about who he was.

practice.q: Contrast identity cohesion and role confusion, and explain what factors affect ego identity and why some people fail to achieve it.
practice.answer:
In adolescence (12–18) we must resolve the crisis of ego identity by integrating our ideas about ourselves with what others think of us. Identity cohesion, the adaptive outcome, is a consistent, congruent self-image; such people face adulthood with certainty and confidence and develop fidelity. Role confusion, the maladaptive outcome of an identity crisis, leaves people not knowing who they are, where they belong or where they are going; they may withdraw from education, work and marriage or adopt a negative identity in crime or drugs.

Several factors affect identity. Earlier stages matter: Waterman et al. found adolescents with trust, autonomy, initiative and industriousness achieved identity cohesion. A psychological moratorium for experimenting with roles is needed. Peer groups have a strong impact; fanatical groups, cults or obsessive celebrity identification restrict the ego. Parenting matters: loving but directive parents foster identity achievement. Social and historical forces, gender, ethnicity, activities such as sport and volunteering, college attendance and online role-play also play a part.

People fail when earlier crises were resolved maladaptively, when they lack opportunity to experiment (Slugoski and Ginsburg note the moratorium may be unaffordable for the poor), or when they are cut off from their culture.

practice.q: What are the two ways of adapting to maturity and old age, how can the positive way be achieved, and what role does generativity play in it?
practice.answer:
In the final stage (55+), people evaluate their whole life and adapt through ego integrity or despair. Ego integrity means looking back with fulfilment, accepting one's place and past and believing one has coped with victories and failures. Despair means frustration, anger at missed opportunities, regret over unfixable mistakes, self-disgust, contempt for others and bitterness.

In Vital Involvement in Old Age, based on 29 people in their 80s, Erikson prescribed staying active and vitally involved: seeking challenge and stimulation through grandparenting, returning to school and developing new skills and interests, not merely reflecting on the past.

As an old man Erikson concluded that generativity was even more important than he had first thought; much of older people's despair is really continued stagnation. Generativity developed in the seventh stage may be the most important contributor to ego integrity. Research agrees: continued family and community involvement sustains generativity into old age (Warburton et al.), while Hong Kong elders who felt obsolete with technology lost generativity (Cheng). Life review, reminiscence and acknowledging regrets are also linked to ego integrity, which brings well-being, less fear of death and the strength of wisdom.

practice.q: Based on his play-constructions research, what did Erikson conclude about sex differences in personality? Evaluate the conclusion.
practice.answer:
Erikson asked boys and girls aged 10 to 12 to build a scene from an imaginary movie using dolls, toy animals, cars and blocks. Girls built static, peaceful, low enclosed structures that intruders (male or animal figures) tried to enter; boys built tall towers and scenes of action, cars and moving people.

As an orthodox Freudian, Erikson concluded that these differences paralleled genital anatomy: the external, intrusive male organ versus the internal female organs. Biology, he implied, determined that girls build enclosures and boys build towers, so sex differences in personality were anatomically based.

This conclusion has been strongly criticised for implying that women are victims of their anatomy, their personalities shaped by the absence of a penis. The differences could equally reflect cultural sex-role training, in which girls are taught to be less action-oriented, aggressive and achievement-oriented. Erikson himself later admitted this possibility. Later research supports the social explanation: gender-typed toy preferences persist and are taught by parents, especially fathers, who reward passivity in girls and assertiveness in boys. The anatomical interpretation is therefore poorly supported.

practice.q: How can the conflicts of the three adult stages be resolved in positive ways?
practice.answer: Intimacy vs. isolation is resolved by forming caring, committed relationships in which one merges identity with another without losing it (strength: love). Generativity vs. stagnation is resolved by teaching, mentoring and guiding the next generation through family, work or institutions (care). Ego integrity vs. despair is resolved by accepting one's past and staying vitally involved (wisdom).

summary: Erikson, trained by Anna Freud without any degree, extended Freud: life-span development, an independent ego, and cultural and historical influences.
His own identity crises (unknown father, rejection at school, years of wandering) shaped his concept of the identity crisis.
He observed identity confusion in uprooted American Indians and WWII veterans.
Eight psychosocial stages follow the epigenetic principle: genes set the stages, the environment determines how they unfold.
Each stage has a crisis with adaptive and maladaptive ways of coping; a mostly adaptive but balanced resolution yields a basic strength.
Stages and strengths: trust/hope, autonomy/will, initiative/purpose, industriousness/competence, identity/fidelity, intimacy/love, generativity/care, integrity/wisdom.
Outcomes of the first four stages depend on others; in the last four we have increasing conscious choice.
Maldevelopment: only the adaptive tendency = maladaptive (neuroses); only the negative = malignant (psychoses); both treatable.
Erikson's view of human nature is optimistic, partially deterministic and emphasises learning over heredity.
Assessment: play therapy, anthropological studies and psychohistorical analysis; later tests include the Loyola Generativity Scale.
Research supports early trust, the stage sequence, Marcia's identity statuses and the benefits of generativity and ego integrity.
The identity crisis may continue into the twenties and college can prolong the moratorium.
Ethnic identity (Cross model) and gender preference identity (Frable) develop in stages and affect ego identity.
Criticisms: vague concepts, incomplete maturity stage, anatomical view of sex differences, poor fit to women and the poor.
His influence includes life-span developmental psychology and play therapy with abused children.
